title: Protocol Selection
subtitle: Choose targets from goals, evidence, safety and measurable hypotheses
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating protocol selection within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain protocol selection without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in protocol selection.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to protocol selection.

sections.explainSimply: A protocol specifies what signal is trained, where, how and toward what functional goal.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Selection should integrate referral goals, symptom formulation, raw EEG quality, medical risk, evidence, feasibility and patient preference.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: QEEG can contribute hypotheses, but map normalisation is not itself a validated outcome. Use a testable rationale and predefined review points.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A rehabilitation plan: define the target, dose, measurement and stopping rule before changing the exercise.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand protocol selection to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Protocol shopping after every difficult session prevents interpretable learning.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using protocol selection predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Protocol shopping after every difficult session prevents interpretable learning. Evidence classification: clinical reasoning; evidence varies by protocol.
